video.title: I make $25K/month from one simple website

summary: Roman describes CareerHound, a subscription job board that scrapes listings from company websites for US jobseekers. He reports $25K in one introduction and later says the business made $28,000 in total revenue last month, with $12K MRR; the transcript does not explain the difference. His central growth method is researching audience interests, repeating timeless social content formats, and giving creators clear briefs. The main takeaway is that he credits marketing and distribution, more than product novelty, for the business’s growth.

speakers.name: Gus
speakers.description: Starter Story host; introduces himself as Gus.

ideas.name: CareerHound job board
ideas.one_liner: A paid job board that scrapes listings from company websites and uses social content to attract jobseekers.
ideas.business_model: Recurring subscriptions with weekly, monthly, and annual plans behind a hard paywall.
ideas.customer: People in the US who are looking for a job, whether employed or unemployed.
ideas.problem: Jobseekers want to find relevant openings, including remote roles and jobs listed directly on company websites.
ideas.offer: A job board that scrapes jobs directly from company websites. Roman also promotes lists of companies hiring remotely and worldwide through social content that directs viewers to CareerHound.

pricing.model: Recurring subscription; hard paywall with no free plan.
pricing.notes: Roman states the prices without naming the currency; USD is used because CareerHound targets US users.

acquisition_channels.details: Roman researches content in his niche across Instagram, Reddit, and TikTok, then uses repeatable formats such as lists of companies hiring remotely and worldwide, ending with a call to visit CareerHound.

quote.text: In my niche, people will always want to find companies hiring remotely and worldwide. So I can keep running this list over and over and over again.
quote.speaker: Roman

acquisition_channels.details: Roman pays creators to make content for CareerHound. The transcript does not say whether the content is boosted as paid advertising or posted organically by creators.

quote.text: And I'll often send a message saying, "Hey, you wanna do some paid content work." In like 90% of situations, you don't wanna pay more than $20 a video.
quote.speaker: Roman

acquisition_channels.details: Roman uses creator marketplaces to find people who can make promotional content; he does not name a specific marketplace for this process.

quote.text: The easiest way is to use a marketplace. There are a bunch of creator marketplaces.
quote.speaker: Roman

acquisition_channels.details: Roman says he finds creators by scrolling and DMing people who already make content. This is creator recruitment, not stated customer outreach; unsolicited DMs to UK individuals or sole traders require care under PECR.

quote.text: But most of my creators, I find just by DMing people. They scroll, scroll, and scroll, and I find people who are already making content just for fun.
quote.speaker: Roman

ideas.delivery: The website scrapes job listings from company websites and presents them on the job board. The transcript does not describe the scraping system, listing review, customer onboarding, or support process. Creators make social content using Roman's instructed formats.
unit_economics_claims: Roman says the average user lifetime value is $50.
Roman reports 31% churn, explaining that job search is a high-turnover product.
Roman reports $28,000 total revenue last month and $12K MRR; an earlier statement says $25K last month.
Roman says there were over 8,079 active subscriptions.
Roman says creators generally should not be paid more than $20 per video in 90% of situations.
tools: Hetzner (heard in the transcript as “head snare”)

acquisition.how: Agents can research topics, draft content, and schedule posts, but spotting useful formats and managing creator work need judgment. The described unsolicited creator DMs should not be automated to UK individuals without consent.

onboarding.how: A paid subscription site can grant access after checkout. Roman does not describe the account setup or onboarding steps.

delivery.how: A scraper can collect and publish job listings automatically, but scraping failures and stale listings need routine checks.

billing.how: Weekly, monthly, and annual subscriptions fit recurring billing software; the payment provider and billing operations are not stated.

support.how: The support process is not stated. Agents could handle routine subscription questions, with human review for billing problems and listing complaints.

uk_applicability.notes: The job-board and subscription model could work in the UK, but CareerHound targets US jobseekers. A UK version would need UK job sources and local pricing, plus attention to privacy, scraping, and employment-related requirements. Unsolicited creator DMs to individuals or sole traders need consent under UK PECR.

risks: Roman reports 31% churn and says it is high because job search is a short-term need, which can make ongoing customer acquisition important.
Scraped listings can become stale or unavailable, and the transcript does not describe how CareerHound checks listing accuracy or handles source-site restrictions.
Social reach depends on content performance and platform distribution; the reported 11.7 million views are not guaranteed to repeat.
Creator content requires clear briefs and ongoing creator management.
Unsolicited marketing DMs to UK individuals and sole traders are restricted by PECR without consent; automated creator outreach would need a compliant approach.

tactics.name: Research for timeless content formats
steps: Spend substantial time reviewing niche content across Instagram, Reddit, and TikTok.
Review both video and text rather than limiting research to one format.
Save examples that catch your attention and investigate what makes them work.
Look for recurring audience interests and questions that can support repeatable content.

quote.text: And I call it content thrifting, basically as you scroll and go through all of this content, you're just accumulating a bunch of stuff that grabs your attention
quote.speaker: Roman

tactics.name: Repeat formats that convert
steps: Find a format that matches a durable audience desire, such as remote and worldwide job listings.
Use a clear hook, list the companies that fit the promise, and end with a call to visit the website.
Repeat the format while it continues to work, instead of chasing every short-lived trend.

quote.text: In my niche, people will always want to find companies hiring remotely and worldwide. So I can keep running this list over and over and over again.
quote.speaker: Roman

tactics.name: Give creators simple, specific briefs
steps: Put repeatable content formats and instructions in a sheet.
Review each brief for points that could confuse a creator.
Reduce research and production work so a first-time creator can follow the format.

quote.text: It's zero research. All they have to do is open up their laptop and there's a sheet of formats perfectly instructed.
quote.speaker: Roman

tactics.name: Source creators through marketplaces and existing content
steps: Try creator marketplaces as a source.
Scroll through platforms and look for people already making content for fun.
Offer paid content work and keep video costs low; Roman recommends a ceiling of $20 in most situations.
Choose creators whose apparent credibility fits the audience and topic.

quote.text: But most of my creators, I find just by DMing people. They scroll, scroll, and scroll, and I find people who are already making content just for fun.
quote.speaker: Roman

tactics.name: Use existing spend and app demand to find product directions
steps: Use Side Shift to see what companies are hiring creators.
Treat companies paying for creator work as a signal that they have a budget and are making money.
Use Sensor Tower to find apps getting downloads.
Choose a product direction you personally enjoy, then use existing content as marketing inspiration.

quote.text: One creative way to source product ideas is to sign up on side shift, which is a creator marketplace.
quote.speaker: Roman

tactics.name: Run frequent marketing experiments and learn from failures
steps: Run marketing experiments frequently.
Record what happened in each experiment, including failed attempts.
Extract a lesson from each result and use it to choose the next experiment.

quote.text: So you wanna strive for failed results because this way you can eliminate what doesn't work and get closer to the thing that's gonna work.
quote.speaker: Roman

tactics.name: Start with a hard paywall
steps: Offer paid weekly, monthly, and annual subscriptions.
Do not offer a free plan, according to Roman's current approach.

quote.text: So I'm a strong believer in a hard paywall, so no free plans. Our users pay $7 a week, 20 a month, or 50 a year.

warnings.warning: Job search is a short-term use case; Roman says CareerHound has 31% churn.

warnings.warning: Unsolicited marketing DMs to UK individuals or sole traders require consent under PECR, so the creator-sourcing approach needs a compliant route in the UK.

lessons.lesson: Start by understanding the audience's recurring questions and problems, then make content that addresses them.

quote.text: What are their fundamental questions and problems? And then I solve for those questions and problems using content.
quote.speaker: Roman

lessons.lesson: Build distribution around enduring audience interests; trend-only content creates a constant production chase.

quote.text: And if you build your distribution system on timely content, it's a constant grind chase after trends.
quote.speaker: Roman

lessons.lesson: Research across platforms and formats to notice patterns other marketers may miss.

quote.text: And in order to have a breakthrough in content, you need to spot something that's not obvious to other people
quote.speaker: Roman

lessons.lesson: Once a content format converts, repeat it while the audience continues to want the outcome it promises.

quote.text: So the key to escape the hamster wheel in UGC, in content marketing is to discover formats that are converting and repeatable.
quote.speaker: Roman

lessons.lesson: Match creator credibility to the audience and make the content brief clear enough for inexperienced creators to execute.

quote.text: When I'm designing the instructions for their content, I'm asking myself, have I left any room for confusion? Or is it super simple?
quote.speaker: Roman

lessons.lesson: Use real market signals, such as companies paying for creator work or apps gaining downloads, to choose product directions.

quote.text: And look at what companies are hiring creators because these companies have money, pay them, which means they're making money.
quote.speaker: Roman

lessons.lesson: Treat failed marketing experiments as useful information and change the next attempt based on what you learn.

quote.text: So you wanna strive for failed results because this way you can eliminate what doesn't work and get closer to the thing that's gonna work.
quote.speaker: Roman

lessons.lesson: A simple product can compete when its distribution and marketing are strong.

quote.text: I think what makes me stand out has nothing to do with the product. It all has to do with my ability to spike people's emotions, to make people think things in their heads through my content.
quote.speaker: Roman

lessons.lesson: Keep faith during the early stage and build a consistent habit of testing and learning.

quote.text: I think once you make your first money online, it becomes really obvious that you can do it.
quote.speaker: Roman

evidence_quality.rationale: Roman gives first-hand operating details, subscription prices, customer and churn figures, revenue claims, and a concrete content and creator workflow. The transcript includes different figures for last month's revenue ($25K and $28,000), and the claims are not independently verified here.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Starter Story promotes its free database of simple apps and websites during the video. No Roman course or software product is stated.
